title: The month of Jeth
hook: in Jeth, join with the One before whom all bow (Barah Maha, ang 134)

segments.voice: Yesterday, Vaisakh: the harvest month, when longing points to what's missing. The harvest is in. Now the heat arrives, and the third month asks for something new.

By late morning the roads shimmer. Shops pull their shutters halfway down. This is Jeth, roughly May into June in Punjab, hot in a way that changes how people live. Anyone who can stays indoors through the afternoon, and the dust storms called aandhi can turn the sky brown. In that heat, even the proudest person slows down and looks for shade. Nobody walks tall at two in the afternoon in Jeth. And this is the month Guru Arjan chooses to talk about the One before whom every head goes down.
screen: `MAY INTO JUNE: THE ROADS SHIMMER.` → `EVERYONE LOOKS FOR SHADE.` → `EVERY HEAD GOES DOWN.`

segments.voice: The Jeth stanza is on ang 134. It opens, in paraphrase: in Jeth, the longing is to be joined with the Lord, before whom everyone bows. Not some. Everyone. Kings and laborers, the clever and the simple, the powerful and the poor are all, sooner or later, lowered. The heat makes that easy to picture. Then an image of safety: one who holds the hem of the beloved Friend's robe can't be bound by anyone. It's an old picture, a child or a petitioner clinging to the edge of someone's garment, and protected. Then a picture of riches. The Name of the One is like rubies and pearls, and no thief can break in to steal them. In an old village, valuables could be stolen and houses broken into. Here is wealth no one can carry off. The stanza goes on: the One does whatever pleases the One, and creatures act accordingly; those the One makes His own are called blessed. And it ends: in Jeth, the joyful Lord is met by the one whose forehead carries that good fortune. Put the pieces together: bowing, holding on, a treasure that can't be stolen. Jeth's lesson isn't about pushing through the heat on your own strength. It's about lowering yourself and holding on. In a month when everything outside presses down, the stanza turns the pressure into a bow.
screen: `BEFORE WHOM EVERYONE BOWS.` · `HOLDING THE HEM OF THE FRIEND.` · `JEWELS NO THIEF CAN STEAL.` · `THE PRESSURE BECOMES A BOW.` · then, large: `JETH: BOW.`

segments.voice: Notice one pressure on you right now, tiredness, a deadline, real heat, a weight in the chest, and don't push against it. Breathe in, and as you breathe out, lower your head slowly, as if bowing to something greater than the pressure; stay low a breath or two, picturing the edge of a friend's robe in your hand, then rise. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as you bow.
Jeth. The month of hard heat, when Guru Arjan longs to be joined with the One before whom everyone bows, whose Name is a treasure no thief can steal.
Your line: jeth: bow. Some treasures are out of every thief's reach. That's five hundred sixty-eight.

howItsDone: On the sangrand of Jeth, gurdwaras that keep the day read the Jeth stanza of Guru Arjan's Barah Maha, and in the summer heat, especially around the remembrance of Guru Arjan's martyrdom, Sikhs set up chhabeel stalls serving cold sweetened water to passersby.
